title: Bayesian updating
dek: Posterior ∝ likelihood × prior. The likelihood is the same object the MLE used. The prior is the extra scientific statement you have to defend.
story: Bayes’ theorem on parameters is p(θ | y) = f(y | θ) p(θ) / m(y), where m(y) = ∫ f(y | θ) p(θ) dθ. Everything that was a likelihood in the frequentist plate is still here. The new claim is that θ is a random variable with a prior you are willing to write down.

A posterior mean is a different estimator than an MLE. With a lot of data and a prior that is not insane, they meet. With sparse DST errors, rare mutations, or a new drug, they do not, and that is the point of being Bayesian rather than the embarrassment.

A 95% credible interval is a region with posterior probability 0.95. It is not a 95% confidence interval, which is a statement about long-run coverage of a procedure. You can prefer either; you cannot rename one as the other in a paper.
deepTitle: Priors, conjugacy, and the computation you actually run
deep: Conjugate example: Y ~ Binomial(n, π), π ~ Beta(a, b). Posterior is Beta(a + y, b + n − y). The MLE y/n is the posterior mode as a,b → 1 (uniform) in this parameterization, and the posterior mean (a+y)/(a+b+n) shrinks toward the prior mean a/(a+b).

Nonconjugate models (most GLMs, most phylogenetics) need MCMC, variational inference, or Laplace/INLA. Diagnostics (R̂, ESS, divergences in HMC) are part of the result. A pretty density plot from an unconverged chain is not a posterior.

Prior elicitation in a genomics lab is often hierarchical rather than a single Beta: mutation-specific effects shrunk toward a drug-specific mean, drug means shrunk toward a class. That is the next plate. A “flat prior on the probability scale” can be surprisingly informative on the logit scale, and vice versa.

Model comparison: Bayes factors are ratios of marginal likelihoods. They are not LRTs. WAIC/LOO are predictive criteria closer in spirit to AIC. Mixing a Bayes factor with a p-value in one sentence is a category error.

Priors are scientific statements (own plate). Conjugacy is arithmetic when the kernel closes. Calibration is whether 80% intervals cover 80% of the time under a named DGP. MCMC is how you compute when the kernel does not close. None of those is optional garnish on a “Bayesian analysis” caption.

formulas.label: Bayes on parameters
formulas.note: Normalize by the marginal m(y) if you need a density rather than a score.

formulas.label: Beta–Binomial conjugate
formulas.expression: π | y ~ Beta(a + y, b + n − y)
formulas.note: The likelihood updates the two Beta counts as if they were extra successes and failures.

visual.caption: A weakly informative prior, a likelihood peaked by data, and the posterior compromise. With n large the posterior follows the likelihood; with n small it does not — that is a feature.

example.title: Beta–Binomial for a rare BDQ allele
example.setup: In a new survey, y = 1 isolate with an atpE mutation among n = 80 BDQ-naïve RR-TB genomes. Prior from a previous lab: π ~ Beta(2, 98), mean 2%. Update.

steps.title: Posterior
steps.body: π | y ~ Beta(2+1, 98+79) = Beta(3, 177). Posterior mean 3/180 = 1.67%. MLE is 1/80 = 1.25%. The prior still has a vote because events are rare.

steps.title: Interval
steps.body: A 95% equal-tail credible interval from Beta(3,177) is a statement about posterior probability, not about 95% coverage of a procedure. Quote it as such.

steps.title: Sensitivity
steps.body: If a skeptic uses Beta(1,1), the posterior mean becomes 2/82 ≈ 2.4%. If they use a prior mean of 10% with the same prior strength, the answer moves. Report that sensitivity when n_events = 1.

example.takeaway: With one event, the prior is part of the result. Hide it and you are doing theatre.

check.prompt: A posterior density p(θ | y) requires:
choices: Only a likelihood; the prior is optional decoration
A likelihood and a prior (and a dominating measure), normalized by the marginal
check.answer: A likelihood and a prior (and a dominating measure), normalized by the marginal
check.why: No prior, no posterior. Unbiasedness and n > 30 are frequentist side quests.

whyWrong.That θ̂ be unbiased: Bayesian estimators have other justifications (calibration, Bayes risk).
whyWrong.That n > 30: Small n is often why you wanted a prior.

check.prompt: π ~ Beta(1,1), then y = 4 successes in n = 10 Bernoulli trials. Posterior mean?
check.why: Beta(1,1) → Beta(5, 7). Mean = 5/(5+7) = 5/12 ≈ 0.417. The MLE is 0.4; the uniform prior adds one imaginary success and one failure in this parameterization.

whyWrong.0.4: That is the MLE y/n, not the Beta(5,7) mean.
whyWrong.0.5: That is the prior mean, pre-data.
whyWrong.1: That would be a degenerate posterior.

check.prompt: On the updating plate, the posterior curve sits between prior and likelihood. What scientific claim is that geometry making?
choices: That the posterior is a compromise whose location depends on prior weight versus data weight
That credible intervals have exact 95% frequentist coverage by construction
That the prior must always be narrower than the likelihood
check.answer: That the posterior is a compromise whose location depends on prior weight versus data weight
check.why: With a modest n the prior still pulls. That is visible in the plate as a posterior mean between the two peaks.

whyWrong.That Bayes ignores the data: The likelihood peak is clearly informing the posterior.
whyWrong.That the prior must always be narrower t: Often the opposite in the weakly informative regime.
